bp: This tutorial serves a practical trust problem in open social science: a published method is not fully shared if another researcher can only read the code but cannot run it. Many analyses now live in notebooks, scripts, and repositories. Those files may contain the real method: how data is loaded, cleaned, transformed, checked, and displayed. But a second reader also needs the surrounding machine setup, including the right software packages, versions, folder layout, and instructions. The GESIS Methods Hub is presented as a place for well-documented methodological contributions, while Jupyter4NFDI and MyBinder supply executable examples that can open in a browser. The real object being improved is therefore not a model or dataset but the research artifact itself. The tutorial asks how to turn an existing analysis, notebook, or code repository into something self-contained enough that a user can click, run, inspect, and reuse it.
wh: The hard part is that code depends on many things that are usually invisible. A notebook may look complete, yet it may assume a local file path, a package installed months ago, a system library on the author's laptop, or a startup command the author never wrote down. GitHub stores files, but it does not automatically explain how those files should become a working session. MyBinder adds another constraint: it has to build a temporary runnable environment from the repository description. If the repository layout is unclear, if required packages are missing, or if the environment instructions contradict each other, the build fails before the method can be tested. Social science methods add another pressure: the point is not merely to execute code, but to preserve enough methodological context that the computation still means what the author claims. Reproducibility fails when any one link is implicit.
naive: A smart beginner would put the notebook and scripts on GitHub, add a short README, and assume that this is sharing. That helps with visibility, but it leaves the reader doing detective work. They must guess which software to install, which file to open first, where data should sit, and whether errors come from their mistake or from missing instructions. Another beginner move is to paste installation commands into a document without testing them in a fresh machine. That also fails because the instructions may only work on the author's computer. The tutorial exists because reproducible execution requires a repository that a service can rebuild from stated rules, not just a folder that humans can browse.
ap: The core idea is to treat a method repository as a small, portable machine rather than as a loose pile of files. The tutorial teaches participants to make the pieces that MyBinder and Methods Hub need explicit: a clear repository structure, an executable example, a specification of the computational environment, and checks for common build failures. MyBinder is the execution side: it reads the repository, constructs a temporary browser-accessible workspace, and lets the user run the notebook or code without manual installation. Methods Hub is the publication and reuse side: it combines documentation of the methodological contribution with that executable example. The central move is therefore packaging. The author takes an existing analysis and turns hidden local assumptions into public, testable instructions, so the method becomes a one-click resource rather than a personal setup.
mech: The mechanism starts with one existing method: perhaps an analysis notebook, a script collection, or a code repository. First, the participant identifies the intended entry point: the notebook or command that a new user should run to see the method work. Second, the repository is organized so that this entry point, supporting code, data examples, and documentation sit in predictable places. Third, the computational environment is described. In plain terms, this means listing the software ingredients that must be present before the method can run, such as language versions and packages, instead of relying on whatever happens to be installed locally. Fourth, MyBinder reads those instructions and tries to build a fresh runnable workspace from the repository. This is the crucial test because it simulates a stranger arriving without the author's laptop. Fifth, failures are diagnosed: missing packages, unclear paths, incompatible versions, oversized or unavailable resources, or notebooks that require unstated manual steps. Sixth, the working repository is connected to the Methods Hub as a documented methodological contribution with an executable example. The output is not a new statistical result. It is a self-contained research method that can be opened, run, inspected, and reused through a stable publication workflow.
math: This tutorial is not proposing a numerical algorithm, but it still rests on precise system ideas. The first is information preservation: a computation can be repeated only if the necessary setup information survives outside the author's head. The repository must keep not just code, but also the instructions that turn code into a working process. The second is constraint satisfaction, which means that a build succeeds only when several conditions are true at once: files are named where the runner expects them, packages are available, versions can live together, and the executable example starts without hidden manual work. One broken condition can stop the whole chain. The third idea is standardization. By using common repository structures, environment files, checklists, and templates, different methods become easier to compare, test, and publish because the reader does not have to learn a new setup language each time. The main tradeoff is completeness versus burden. Too little detail leaves the method fragile; too much custom machinery makes it hard for others to understand or maintain. MyBinder works here as a reproducibility test: it rebuilds the method from public instructions, exposing whether the stated recipe is complete enough.
dots: This tutorial connects to the conference's reproducible research theme and to the neighboring R2CASS workshop in the repo. R2CASS frames reproducibility as a community problem for computational social science, using Methods Hub, guidelines, checklists, templates, and hands-on tasks to lower barriers. This tutorial handles the narrower engineering step inside that larger effort: how an actual repository becomes Methods Hub and MyBinder ready. It also sits beside evaluation and benchmark papers in the broader dataset, because those papers depend on repeatable measurement. A benchmark, retrieval study, recommendation audit, or social media analysis is only useful to the field if another group can rerun enough of the pipeline to understand where the result came from. The shared deeper idea is controlled reuse. Data-mining papers often package data, rankings, models, or evaluations; this tutorial packages the method itself so later readers can execute rather than merely cite it.
ww: The approach works because reproducibility failures are usually concrete rather than mysterious. A method does not become unreliable only because the scientific idea is wrong; it often fails because a package was not named, a file path assumed the author's laptop, a notebook cell depended on an earlier manual action, or a build service could not infer the intended setup. The tutorial's workflow attacks these small breaks before publication. Repository structure gives a new user and an automated builder a map. Environment specification turns private installation history into public instructions. MyBinder supplies a fresh-room test: if the repository can build there, it is much more likely that the method is not secretly tied to one machine. Methods Hub then gives the runnable artifact a publication context, so execution is paired with explanation. This is better than the naive GitHub-only approach because it checks the actual operation the reader cares about: not whether files are visible, but whether the method can be reconstructed and run from those files.
po: The payoff is a practical capability for workshop participants: they should leave able to transform an existing method into a self-contained, one-click executable resource suitable for publication in the GESIS Methods Hub. They also leave with concrete checklists and templates that can be reused on later projects. For the field, the gain is lower friction around open social science. A reader can inspect the method, run the example, and learn from the repository structure instead of spending effort on setup guesswork. The abstract's claimed result is educational and infrastructural: participants learn how MyBinder works, how to structure repositories, and how to avoid build failures.
limits: The abstract supports the tutorial workflow, not an empirical proof that every method can become reproducible with this recipe. It assumes participants can share enough code, example data, and setup information for execution; restricted data, private platform access, unusual hardware, or licensed software may limit what MyBinder can run. It also assumes the repository can be made small and stable enough for a build service. A successful Binder launch shows that the example executes, but it does not prove that the social science interpretation is correct, that the original data collection was sound, or that future package changes will never break the resource.
